passage: Trisha, come and sit. I hear someone told you girls can't play cricket. Let me tell you something. I'm Deepika, your Masi. When I was ten I loved cricket. The boys in our lane said, "Girls don't play, go and skip." It felt so unfair that my chest went hot. But I still went every evening with my bat and stood at the edge of the lane. I asked my father why there was such a rule. He said, "It's how it's always been." I said, "That's not a reason." One day a boy called Imran said, "Let her bowl one." Months later, they had stopped saying it. Keep your bat, Trisha.

qa.q: What did the boys in Deepika's lane say to her?
qa.a: They said, "Girls don't play, go and skip."

qa.q: What did ten-year-old Deepika feel when the boys said girls don't play?
qa.a: She felt angry at how unfair it was, so much that her chest went hot.

qa.q: What did Deepika do that Trisha could also do?
qa.a: She kept doing what she loved, turned up every evening, and asked why the rule existed.

qa.q: How did Deepika's father see her question about the rule?
qa.a: He offered no reason beyond how it had always been, which suggests he had not thought about why the rule exists.

grounding: A girl told girls should not play cricket feels it is unfair, keeps playing and asks why the rule exists, told by an elder.
